Getting started with RCamelsPE

Source: vignettes/rcamelspe.Rmd
rcamelspe.Rmd

Introduction

RCamelsPE is an R package to read, explore and visualize the CAMELS-PE dataset: Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies - Peru. CAMELS-PE provides, for 136 catchments in Peru:

  • station metadata, including the quality control of the observed streamflow;
  • static catchment attributes: topography, climate, hydrological signatures, land cover, geology, soils and human intervention;
  • annual land-cover series (1985-2024) by class and subclass;
  • daily time series (1981-2025) of precipitation from three products, potential evapotranspiration from three formulations, temperature, solar radiation, vapour pressure, and observed and simulated streamflow;
  • catchment boundaries and gauge locations.

This tutorial walks through all of these components. It uses a small sample of the dataset included in the package (two catchments and one year of daily data, 1981), so every example runs without downloading the full dataset. With the full dataset, the same code works for all catchments and the full period.

library(RCamelsPE)
library(ggplot2)

The examples below use a small helper that stacks several columns of a table into long format, which is convenient for plotting several variables with ggplot2:

stack_columns <- function(data, cols, id_cols = c("date", "gauge_id")) {
  out <- lapply(cols, function(col) {
    data.frame(data[id_cols], variable = col, value = data[[col]])
  })
  do.call(rbind, out)
}

1. Getting the data

Download the CAMELS-PE dataset

The dataset is distributed separately from the package through Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20058778; this concept DOI always resolves to the latest version). The package is designed for CAMELS-PE v2.0, which is downloaded and extracted by default:

download_camels_pe(path = "path/to/folder")

download_camels_pe() also defines the dataset path for the current R session. Earlier versions (version = "1.0.1" or "1.0") can be downloaded to reproduce previous studies, but they have a different file structure and variable names.

Set the dataset path

If the dataset was downloaded manually or in a previous session, define its location once per session. All reading functions then use this path:

set_camels_path("path/to/CAMELS-PE")

This tutorial uses the sample dataset:

set_camels_path(camels_path)
get_camels_path()
#> [1] "C:/Users/hllauca/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpSYJWMD/temp_libpath2dd4371a3455/RCamelsPE/extdata/sample_camels_pe"

The dataset is organized in four folders:

CAMELS-PE/
├── 01_metadata/      stations.csv, data_dictionary.csv
├── 02_attributes/    static attributes and annual land-cover series
├── 03_timeseries/    timeseries.csv and by_catchment/<gauge_id>.csv
└── 04_geospatial/    gauges and catchment boundaries (GeoPackage)

2. The data dictionary

Every variable of CAMELS-PE is documented in the data dictionary, with its description, unit, category, file and data source. It is the best starting point to find a variable.

dict <- read_dictionary()
table(dict$category)
#> 
#>           climatic           geologic         geospatial human_intervention 
#>                 11                 24                  3                 17 
#>       hydrological         land_cover           metadata               soil 
#>                 35                 55                 18                 30 
#>         timeseries        topographic 
#>                 41                  8

Filter by category, variable or file:

read_dictionary(category = "timeseries")[, c("variable", "unit", "source")]
#> # A tibble: 41 × 3
#>    variable      unit       source                                            
#>    <chr>         <chr>      <chr>                                             
#>  1 date          YYYY-MM-DD -                                                 
#>  2 gauge_id      -          SENAMHI                                           
#>  3 prec_pisco    mm/day     PISCOp v3.0                                       
#>  4 prec_sd_pisco mm/day     PISCOp v3.0                                       
#>  5 prec_chirps   mm/day     CHIRPS v3 (daily, RNL)                            
#>  6 prec_era5land mm/day     ERA5-Land                                         
#>  7 pet_hs        mm/day     Hargreaves-Samani (FAO-56 Eq. 52) from PISCOt v1.2
#>  8 pet_pt        mm/day     PISCOt v1.2 and ERA5-Land                         
#>  9 pet_ou        mm/day     PISCOt v1.2                                       
#> 10 tmin          degC       PISCOt v1.2                                       
#> # ℹ 31 more rows
read_dictionary(variable = "flow_obs_flag")$description
#> [1] "Quality-control flag of the observed streamflow (QARTOD): 1 pass, 3 suspect (kept), 4 fail (removed), 9 missing"
#> [2] "Quality-control flag of the observed streamflow (QARTOD): 1 pass, 3 suspect (kept), 4 fail (removed), 9 missing"

Search descriptions by keyword:

pet_vars <- dict[grepl("evapotranspiration", dict$description), ]
unique(pet_vars[, c("file", "variable")])
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>   file                      variable
#>   <chr>                     <chr>   
#> 1 climatic_indices.csv      pet_mean
#> 2 timeseries.csv            pet_hs  
#> 3 timeseries.csv            pet_pt  
#> 4 timeseries.csv            pet_ou  
#> 5 by_catchment/PE_xxxxx.csv pet_hs  
#> 6 by_catchment/PE_xxxxx.csv pet_pt  
#> 7 by_catchment/PE_xxxxx.csv pet_ou

3. Station metadata

The station table has one row per catchment, identified by gauge_id:

stations <- read_metadata()
names(stations)
#>  [1] "gauge_id"            "gauge_name"          "gauge_region"       
#>  [4] "gauge_lat"           "gauge_lon"           "gauge_elev"         
#>  [7] "gauge_record_start"  "gauge_record_end"    "gauge_perc_obs"     
#> [10] "flow_obs_n_suspect"  "flow_obs_n_fail"     "flow_obs_perc_fail" 
#> [13] "name_cat"            "is_nested"           "nested_group_id"    
#> [16] "nested_group_size"   "downstream_gauge_id" "upstream_gauge_id"

Gauge coordinates correspond to the catchment outlet, and gauge_elev is the FABDEM elevation at that point:

stations[, c("gauge_id", "gauge_name", "gauge_region",
             "gauge_lat", "gauge_lon", "gauge_elev")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   gauge_id  gauge_name gauge_region gauge_lat gauge_lon gauge_elev
#>   <chr>     <chr>      <chr>            <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900 La Capilla Pacific         -12.5      -76.5        399
#> 2 PE_200907 Racarumi   Pacific          -6.63     -79.3        267

The record period and completeness of the observed streamflow:

stations[, c("gauge_id", "gauge_record_start", "gauge_record_end",
             "gauge_perc_obs")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   gauge_id  gauge_record_start gauge_record_end gauge_perc_obs
#>   <chr>     <date>             <date>                    <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900 1981-01-01         2025-12-31                 83.7
#> 2 PE_200907 1981-01-01         2023-08-31                 94.6

A summary of the quality control of the observed streamflow (Sect. 9) is also stored for each gauge: the number of suspect values (kept) and of values that failed and were removed:

stations[, c("gauge_id", "flow_obs_n_suspect", "flow_obs_n_fail",
             "flow_obs_perc_fail")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   gauge_id  flow_obs_n_suspect flow_obs_n_fail flow_obs_perc_fail
#>   <chr>                  <dbl>           <dbl>              <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900               1199             140               1.01
#> 2 PE_200907                 23               0               0

Some catchments are nested (one gauge lies upstream of another). The nesting columns identify the group and the gauges directly upstream and downstream:

stations[, c("gauge_id", "is_nested", "nested_group_id",
             "nested_group_size", "downstream_gauge_id",
             "upstream_gauge_id")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   gauge_id  is_nested nested_group_id nested_group_size downstream_gauge_id
#>   <chr>     <lgl>     <chr>                       <dbl> <chr>              
#> 1 PE_212900 FALSE     PE_212900                       1 NONE               
#> 2 PE_200907 TRUE      PE_200907                       6 NONE               
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: upstream_gauge_id <chr>

We select one catchment for the rest of the tutorial:

gauge_id <- "PE_212900"

4. Geospatial data

Catchment boundaries and gauge locations are read as sf objects:

catchments <- read_geospatial("catchments")
gauges <- read_geospatial("gauges")
catchments
#> Simple feature collection with 2 features and 10 fields
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -79.32084 ymin: -12.58695 xmax: -75.94115 ymax: -6.35042
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
#>    gauge_id       name                  name_cat     area perimeter is_nested
#> 1 PE_212900 La Capilla               Cuenca Mala 2123.654  277.3470     FALSE
#> 2 PE_200907   Racarumi Cuenca Chancay-Lambayeque 2364.256  266.3648      TRUE
#>   downstream_gauge_id upstream_gauge_id nested_group_id nested_group_size
#> 1                NONE              NONE       PE_212900                 1
#> 2                NONE       PE_47E1D6C2       PE_200907                 6
#>                             geom
#> 1 MULTIPOLYGON (((-76.33093 -...
#> 2 MULTIPOLYGON (((-78.68676 -...

Plot all catchments, or a single catchment with its outlet:

plot_catchments(catchments, gauges)

plot_catchments(catchments, gauges, gauge_id = gauge_id)

plot_attribute_map() colours the catchments by any attribute (Sect. 5):

clim <- read_attributes("climatic")

plot_attribute_map(
  catchments = catchments,
  attributes = clim,
  variable = "aridity",
  gauges = gauges
)

5. Catchment attributes

Static attributes are organized in thematic groups, read with read_attributes(). All tables are keyed by gauge_id and can be filtered with the gauge_id argument.

Topography 

read_attributes("topographic")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   gauge_id   area perimeter elev_min elev_max elev_mean elev_median slope_mean
#>   <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900 2124.      277.     399.    5870.     3542.       3920.       507.
#> 2 PE_200907 2364.      266.     267.    4112.     2350.       2312.       407.

Area and perimeter are in km2 and km, elevations in m a.s.l. and the mean slope in m/km.

Climate

Climatic indices are computed from 1981 to 2025 with the reference products only (PISCOp precipitation and Hargreaves-Samani PET). The alternative precipitation and PET products are provided as time series:

clim[, c("gauge_id", "p_mean", "pet_mean", "aridity")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   gauge_id  p_mean pet_mean aridity
#>   <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900   1.24     3.47    2.79
#> 2 PE_200907   2.44     3.60    1.48

Seasonality and the frequency, duration and timing of high-precipitation and dry days:

clim[, c("gauge_id", "p_seasonality", "high_prec_freq", "high_prec_dur",
         "high_prec_timing", "low_prec_freq", "low_prec_dur",
         "low_prec_timing")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   gauge_id  p_seasonality high_prec_freq high_prec_dur high_prec_timing
#>   <chr>             <dbl>          <dbl>         <dbl> <chr>           
#> 1 PE_212900         1.31            17.0          2.07 DJF             
#> 2 PE_200907         0.714           11.7          1.60 MAM             
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: low_prec_freq <dbl>, low_prec_dur <dbl>,
#> #   low_prec_timing <chr>

Hydrological signatures

Signatures are provided twice: computed from the observed streamflow after quality control ("hydrological") and from the simulated streamflow ("hydrological_sim"). The observed signatures use only hydrological years with enough observations; the columns q_obs_* give the period used.

hyd <- read_attributes("hydrological")
hyd_sim <- read_attributes("hydrological_sim")

hyd[, c("gauge_id", "q_mean", "runoff_ratio", "baseflow_index",
        "q_obs_years", "q_obs_start", "q_obs_end")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   gauge_id q_mean runoff_ratio baseflow_index q_obs_years q_obs_start q_obs_end 
#>   <chr>     <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>       <dbl> <date>      <date>    
#> 1 PE_2129…   0.68        0.54           0.573          33 1981-09-01  2025-08-31
#> 2 PE_2009…   1.30        0.538          0.631          42 1981-09-01  2023-08-31

Both tables share the same column names, which makes it easy to compare observed and simulated signatures:

sig <- c("q_mean", "runoff_ratio", "baseflow_index", "Q5", "Q95",
         "high_q_freq", "low_q_freq")

data.frame(
  signature = sig,
  observed = unlist(hyd[hyd$gauge_id == gauge_id, sig]),
  simulated = unlist(hyd_sim[hyd_sim$gauge_id == gauge_id, sig]),
  row.names = NULL
)
#>        signature observed simulated
#> 1         q_mean    0.680     0.639
#> 2   runoff_ratio    0.540     0.513
#> 3 baseflow_index    0.573     0.595
#> 4             Q5    0.031     0.030
#> 5            Q95    2.787     2.638
#> 6    high_q_freq   72.854    79.432
#> 7     low_q_freq  178.887   182.386

Land cover

Static land-cover attributes refer to the year 2024 (MapBiomas Peru, Ecuador and Colombia). Glaciers and other water bodies are also given separately (water_perc = glacier_perc + water_body_perc):

read_attributes("land_cover")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 10
#>   gauge_id  forest_perc agricul_perc non_forest_perc non_veget_perc water_perc
#>   <chr>           <dbl>        <dbl>           <dbl>          <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900        5.05         7.15            68.3          18.6       0.842
#> 2 PE_200907       22.5         49.7             24.0           3.55      0.243
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: non_identi_perc <dbl>, glacier_perc <dbl>,
#> #   water_body_perc <dbl>, land_dominant_class <chr>

The annual series from 1985 to 2024 are described in Sect. 6.

Geology and soils 

geo <- read_attributes("geologic")
geo[, c("gauge_id", "geol_1st_class", "glim_1st_class_perc",
        "geol_2nd_class", "glim_2nd_class_perc", "carbonate_rocks_perc",
        "geol_porosity", "geol_permeability")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   gauge_id geol_1st_class glim_1st_class_perc geol_2nd_class glim_2nd_class_perc
#>   <chr>    <chr>                        <dbl> <chr>                        <dbl>
#> 1 PE_2129… vi                            71.1 pa                            12.2
#> 2 PE_2009… vi                            42.0 py                            38.1
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: carbonate_rocks_perc <dbl>, geol_porosity <dbl>,
#> #   geol_permeability <dbl>

Soil attributes (DSOLMap, USDA Soil Taxonomy) give the percentage of each soil order and the dominant order, suborder, great group and texture class of each of the three horizons (h1 shallowest, h3 deepest):

soil <- read_attributes("soil")
soil[, c("gauge_id", "soil_dominant_class", "soil_suborder_dominant_class",
         "soil_great_group_dominant_class", "soil_texture_h1_dominant_class",
         "soil_texture_h3_dominant_class")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   gauge_id  soil_dominant_class soil_suborder_dominant_…¹ soil_great_group_dom…²
#>   <chr>     <chr>               <chr>                     <chr>                 
#> 1 PE_212900 inceptisols         ochrepts                  cryochrepts           
#> 2 PE_200907 ultisols            udults                    tropudults            
#> # ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​soil_suborder_dominant_class,
#> #   ²​soil_great_group_dominant_class
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: soil_texture_h1_dominant_class <chr>,
#> #   soil_texture_h3_dominant_class <chr>

The percentages of all suborders, great groups and horizon texture classes are read with read_soil_classes(), which adds the names, order and suborder from the legend (read_soil_legend()):

sub <- read_soil_classes(level = "suborder")
sub[sub$perc > 0, ]
#> # A tibble: 22 × 7
#>    gauge_id  level    class     name      order       suborder  perc
#>    <chr>     <chr>    <chr>     <chr>     <chr>       <chr>    <dbl>
#>  1 PE_212900 suborder udalfs    Udalfs    Alfisols    NA        1.55
#>  2 PE_212900 suborder ustalfs   Ustalfs   Alfisols    NA        1.46
#>  3 PE_212900 suborder argids    Argids    Aridisols   NA        0.18
#>  4 PE_212900 suborder fluvents  Fluvents  Entisols    NA        8.82
#>  5 PE_212900 suborder orthents  Orthents  Entisols    NA        1.27
#>  6 PE_212900 suborder psamments Psamments Entisols    NA       20.1 
#>  7 PE_212900 suborder orthels   Orthels   Gelisols    NA        0.07
#>  8 PE_212900 suborder ochrepts  Ochrepts  Inceptisols NA       66.2 
#>  9 PE_212900 suborder orthox    Orthox    Oxisols     NA        0.02
#> 10 PE_212900 suborder ustox     Ustox     Oxisols     NA        0.02
#> # ℹ 12 more rows

With format = "wide", one level is returned with one column per class, for example the texture of the shallowest horizon:

read_soil_classes(level = "texture_h1", format = "wide")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 13
#>   gauge_id  sand_perc loamy_sand_perc sandy_loam_perc loam_perc silt_loam_perc
#>   <chr>         <dbl>           <dbl>           <dbl>     <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900         0               0           24.9       66.4              0
#> 2 PE_200907         0               0            5.47      29.2              0
#> # ℹ 7 more variables: silt_perc <dbl>, sandy_clay_loam_perc <dbl>,
#> #   clay_loam_perc <dbl>, silty_clay_loam_perc <dbl>, sandy_clay_perc <dbl>,
#> #   silty_clay_perc <dbl>, clay_perc <dbl>

The suborders and great groups follow the DSOLMap legend, which uses names of the USDA Soil Taxonomy prior to 1999 (e.g. Ochrepts). For the horizons, only the USDA texture class is provided.

Human intervention

Human intervention attributes describe accredited water availability (ADH, surface water and groundwater), reservoirs, tailings dams and whether the catchment can be considered near-natural:

human <- read_attributes("human_intervention")
human[, c("gauge_id", "surface_adh_mm", "groundwater_adh_mm", "adh_ratio",
          "reservoir_n", "reservoir_dor", "tailings_dam_n", "near_natural")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   gauge_id surface_adh_mm groundwater_adh_mm adh_ratio reservoir_n reservoir_dor
#>   <chr>             <dbl>              <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 PE_2129…       0.00418            0           0.615            5        0.417 
#> 2 PE_2009…       0.000351           0.000436    0.0605           3        0.0267
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: tailings_dam_n <dbl>, near_natural <dbl>

reservoir_dor (degree of regulation) and adh_ratio are percentages of the mean annual observed streamflow volume. near_natural (1 = no reservoirs, no tailings dams and less than 10% of anthropic land cover) can be used to select catchments with little human influence. Both sample catchments have reservoirs, so neither is near-natural:

table(near_natural = human$near_natural)
#> near_natural
#> 0 
#> 2

All attributes in one table

type = "all" joins all groups by gauge_id (the simulated signatures are excluded because they share column names with the observed ones):

attrs <- read_attributes("all")
dim(attrs)
#> [1]   2 103

This table is convenient for catchment classification or regionalization, for example to relate the runoff ratio to aridity:

attrs[, c("gauge_id", "aridity", "runoff_ratio", "baseflow_index",
          "forest_perc", "near_natural")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   gauge_id  aridity runoff_ratio baseflow_index forest_perc near_natural
#>   <chr>       <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900    2.79        0.54           0.573        5.05            0
#> 2 PE_200907    1.48        0.538          0.631       22.5             0

6. Annual land-cover series

CAMELS-PE includes the annual land cover of each catchment from 1985 to 2024, at two levels: six aggregated classes (the same as in the static attributes) and the MapBiomas subclasses.

Legend

The legend links each MapBiomas code to its subclass and class:

legend <- read_land_cover_legend()
head(legend, 10)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 5
#>    mapbiomas_id class             class_code subclass              subclass_code
#>           <int> <chr>             <chr>      <chr>                 <chr>        
#>  1            3 Forest formation  forest     Forest Formation      forest_forma…
#>  2            4 Forest formation  forest     Dry forest            dry_forest   
#>  3            5 Forest formation  forest     Mangrove              mangrove     
#>  4            6 Forest formation  forest     Flooded forest        flooded_fore…
#>  5            9 Agricultural area agricul    Planted forest        planted_fore…
#>  6           15 Agricultural area agricul    Pasture               pasture      
#>  7           21 Agricultural area agricul    Mosaic of agricultur… mosaic_agri_…
#>  8           35 Agricultural area agricul    Oil palm              oil_palm     
#>  9           40 Agricultural area agricul    Rice                  rice         
#> 10           72 Agricultural area agricul    Other crops           other_crops

Classes 

lc_class <- read_land_cover(level = "class", gauge_id = gauge_id)
head(lc_class)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 9
#>   gauge_id   year forest_perc agricul_perc non_forest_perc non_veget_perc
#>   <chr>     <int>       <dbl>        <dbl>           <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900  1985        9.44         2.55            65.6           20.7
#> 2 PE_212900  1986       10.4          4.60            63.1           20.5
#> 3 PE_212900  1987        9.32         5.04            63.4           21.0
#> 4 PE_212900  1988        6.33         6.65            65.5           20.3
#> 5 PE_212900  1989        6.33         7.33            65.4           19.7
#> 6 PE_212900  1990        6.21         7.07            65.8           19.7
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: water_perc <dbl>, non_identi_perc <dbl>,
#> #   land_dominant_class <chr>
plot_land_cover(lc_class)

Subclasses

The long format returns one row per catchment, year and subclass, with the names from the legend:

lc_sub <- read_land_cover(
  level = "subclass",
  gauge_id = gauge_id,
  format = "long"
)
head(lc_sub)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   gauge_id   year subclass_code    subclass  class_code class mapbiomas_id  perc
#>   <chr>     <int> <chr>            <chr>     <chr>      <chr>        <int> <dbl>
#> 1 PE_212900  1985 forest_formation Forest F… forest     Fore…            3 9.43 
#> 2 PE_212900  1985 dry_forest       Dry fore… forest     Fore…            4 0.017
#> 3 PE_212900  1985 mangrove         Mangrove  forest     Fore…            5 0    
#> 4 PE_212900  1985 flooded_forest   Flooded … forest     Fore…            6 0    
#> 5 PE_212900  1985 planted_forest   Planted … agricul    Agri…            9 0    
#> 6 PE_212900  1985 pasture          Pasture   agricul    Agri…           15 0

Subclasses that never exceed a given percentage of the catchment can be grouped as “Other”:

plot_land_cover(lc_sub, min_perc = 1)

Land-cover change

With the long format, the change between two years is easy to compute:

lc_change <- read_land_cover(
  level = "subclass",
  years = c(1985, 2024),
  format = "long"
)

change <- reshape(
  as.data.frame(lc_change[, c("gauge_id", "subclass", "year", "perc")]),
  idvar = c("gauge_id", "subclass"),
  timevar = "year",
  direction = "wide"
)
change$diff <- change$perc.2024 - change$perc.1985

# Largest changes (percentage points of the catchment area)
change <- change[order(-abs(change$diff)), ]
head(change, 8)
#>     gauge_id                          subclass perc.1985 perc.2024   diff
#> 65 PE_212900 Mosaic of agriculture and pasture     2.549     7.148  4.599
#> 59 PE_212900                  Forest Formation     9.427     5.040 -4.387
#> 7  PE_200907 Mosaic of agriculture and pasture    43.928    47.482  3.554
#> 71 PE_212900                      Rock outcrop     8.040    11.387  3.347
#> 69 PE_212900            Grassland / Herbaceous    40.005    36.908 -3.097
#> 72 PE_212900                         Scrubland    16.860    19.345  2.485
#> 82 PE_212900  Other natural non vegetated area    20.655    18.592 -2.063
#> 5  PE_200907                    Planted forest     3.837     2.031 -1.806

7. Daily time series

Available variables 

ts_dict <- read_dictionary(file = "timeseries.csv")
ts_dict[, c("variable", "unit", "source")]
#> # A tibble: 21 × 3
#>    variable      unit       source                                            
#>    <chr>         <chr>      <chr>                                             
#>  1 date          YYYY-MM-DD -                                                 
#>  2 gauge_id      -          SENAMHI                                           
#>  3 prec_pisco    mm/day     PISCOp v3.0                                       
#>  4 prec_sd_pisco mm/day     PISCOp v3.0                                       
#>  5 prec_chirps   mm/day     CHIRPS v3 (daily, RNL)                            
#>  6 prec_era5land mm/day     ERA5-Land                                         
#>  7 pet_hs        mm/day     Hargreaves-Samani (FAO-56 Eq. 52) from PISCOt v1.2
#>  8 pet_pt        mm/day     PISCOt v1.2 and ERA5-Land                         
#>  9 pet_ou        mm/day     PISCOt v1.2                                       
#> 10 tmin          degC       PISCOt v1.2                                       
#> # ℹ 11 more rows

The time series include:

  • precipitation from three products: prec_pisco (PISCOp v3.0, reference), prec_chirps (CHIRPS v3) and prec_era5land (ERA5-Land), plus the spatial standard deviation of PISCOp within the catchment (prec_sd_pisco);
  • potential evapotranspiration from three formulations: pet_hs (Hargreaves-Samani, reference), pet_pt (Priestley-Taylor) and pet_ou (Oudin);
  • temperature (tmin, tmean, tmax), solar radiation (srad) and vapour pressure (vprp);
  • observed streamflow after quality control (flow_obs, flow_obs_m3s), before quality control (flow_obs_raw) and its quality-control flag and test (flow_obs_flag, flow_obs_qc_test);
  • simulated streamflow (flow_sim, flow_sim_m3s).

Reading modes

The recommended mode reads one file per catchment, so only the requested catchments are loaded:

ts <- read_timeseries(gauge_id = gauge_id)
dim(ts)
#> [1] 365  21

The global mode reads timeseries.csv, which contains all catchments. With vars, only the requested columns are read, which saves time and memory with the full dataset:

ts_global <- read_timeseries(
  global = TRUE,
  vars = c("date", "gauge_id", "prec_pisco", "flow_obs")
)
head(ts_global)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   date       gauge_id  prec_pisco flow_obs
#>   <date>     <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 1981-01-01 PE_200907      0.027    0.492
#> 2 1981-01-02 PE_200907      0.899    0.462
#> 3 1981-01-03 PE_200907      1.48     0.437
#> 4 1981-01-04 PE_200907      0.203    0.580
#> 5 1981-01-05 PE_200907      0.169    0.475
#> 6 1981-01-06 PE_200907      0.585    0.450

Both modes accept several gauges and a selection of variables:

ts_multi <- read_timeseries(
  gauge_id = stations$gauge_id,
  vars = c("date", "gauge_id", "prec_pisco", "pet_hs", "flow_obs")
)
table(ts_multi$gauge_id)
#> 
#> PE_200907 PE_212900 
#>       365       365

plot_timeseries() plots one variable, with one panel per gauge:

plot_timeseries(ts_multi, variable = "prec_pisco", linewidth = 0.4)

8. Meteorological forcing

Precipitation products

The three precipitation products can be compared directly:

prec_cols <- c("prec_pisco", "prec_chirps", "prec_era5land")

colSums(ts[, prec_cols], na.rm = TRUE)
#>    prec_pisco   prec_chirps prec_era5land 
#>       500.937       451.056      1338.894

Cumulative precipitation shows where the products diverge:

prec_long <- stack_columns(ts, prec_cols)
prec_long$value[is.na(prec_long$value)] <- 0
prec_long$cumulative <- ave(prec_long$value, prec_long$variable, FUN = cumsum)

ggplot(prec_long, aes(date, cumulative, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cumulative precipitation (mm)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

Monthly totals of each product:

prec_long$month <- as.Date(format(prec_long$date, "%Y-%m-01"))
prec_month <- aggregate(value ~ month + variable, data = prec_long, FUN = sum)

ggplot(prec_month, aes(month, value, fill = variable)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Monthly precipitation (mm)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

The spatial standard deviation of PISCOp (prec_sd_pisco) describes how variable precipitation is within the catchment on each day:

ggplot(ts, aes(date)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = pmax(prec_pisco - prec_sd_pisco, 0),
        ymax = prec_pisco + prec_sd_pisco),
    fill = "grey80"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = prec_pisco), colour = "#1f78b4", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Precipitation (mm/day)",
       subtitle = "PISCOp catchment mean +/- spatial standard deviation") +
  theme_bw()

Potential evapotranspiration

The three PET formulations differ mainly in their level:

pet_cols <- c("pet_hs", "pet_pt", "pet_ou")

colMeans(ts[, pet_cols], na.rm = TRUE)
#>   pet_hs   pet_pt   pet_ou 
#> 3.410310 4.163825 2.429370
pet_long <- stack_columns(ts, pet_cols)

ggplot(pet_long, aes(date, value, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "PET (mm/day)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

The choice of the precipitation product and of the PET formulation changes the aridity index (PET / P). For the sample year:

p <- colMeans(ts[, prec_cols], na.rm = TRUE)
e <- colMeans(ts[, pet_cols], na.rm = TRUE)

aridity <- outer(e, p, "/")
round(aridity, 2)
#>        prec_pisco prec_chirps prec_era5land
#> pet_hs       2.48        2.76          0.93
#> pet_pt       3.03        3.37          1.14
#> pet_ou       1.77        1.97          0.66

Temperature, radiation and vapour pressure 

temp_long <- stack_columns(ts, c("tmin", "tmean", "tmax"))

ggplot(temp_long, aes(date, value, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(tmin = "#2c7bb6", tmean = "grey30",
                                 tmax = "#d7191c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Air temperature (degrees C)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

plot_timeseries(ts, variable = "srad")

plot_timeseries(ts, variable = "vprp")

9. Observed streamflow and quality control

Units

Streamflow is given in mm/day (flow_obs, flow_sim), which allows the comparison of catchments of different size and with precipitation and PET, and in m3/s (flow_obs_m3s, flow_sim_m3s):

plot_timeseries(ts, variable = "flow_obs_m3s")

Quality-control flags

The observed streamflow went through an automatic quality control based on the QARTOD tests (gross range, spike, flat line and detection of linearly interpolated values). Each daily value has a flag:

flow_obs_flag Meaning
1 pass
3 suspect: kept in flow_obs, but worth checking
4 fail: removed from flow_obs (set to NA), kept in flow_obs_raw
9 missing

flow_obs_qc_test names the test that raised the flag (only for flags 3 and 4), for example flat_line_suspect (constant values during 7 to 30 days) or flat_line (more than 30 days, removed).

table(flag = ts$flow_obs_flag, useNA = "ifany")
#> flag
#>   1   3   9 
#> 342  22   1
table(test = ts$flow_obs_qc_test, useNA = "ifany")
#> test
#> flat_line_suspect              <NA> 
#>                22               343

Plot the flagged values on top of the series:

flags <- ts[ts$flow_obs_flag %in% c(3, 4), ]
flags$flag <- factor(flags$flow_obs_flag, levels = c(3, 4),
                     labels = c("suspect (3)", "fail (4)"))

ggplot(ts, aes(date, flow_obs_raw)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(
    data = flags,
    aes(colour = flag),
    size = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("suspect (3)" = "#fdae61",
                                 "fail (4)" = "#d7191c"),
                      drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Observed streamflow (mm/day)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

Using the flags

flow_obs is ready to use: values that failed are already removed. Users who prefer a stricter selection can also remove suspect values:

ts$flow_obs_strict <- ifelse(ts$flow_obs_flag == 1, ts$flow_obs, NA)

c(
  flow_obs = sum(!is.na(ts$flow_obs)),
  flow_obs_strict = sum(!is.na(ts$flow_obs_strict))
)
#>        flow_obs flow_obs_strict 
#>             364             342

The original record is kept in flow_obs_raw, so the effect of the quality control can always be checked:

changed <- which(ts$flow_obs_raw != ts$flow_obs |
                   (is.na(ts$flow_obs) & !is.na(ts$flow_obs_raw)))
length(changed)
#> [1] 0

For the full dataset, the number of suspect and failed values per gauge is summarized in the station table (Sect. 3).

10. Observed and simulated streamflow

Simulated streamflow is available for all catchments and days, also where observations are missing:

q_long <- stack_columns(ts, c("flow_obs", "flow_sim"))

ggplot(q_long, aes(date, value, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(flow_obs = "black", flow_sim = "#e31a1c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Streamflow (mm/day)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

Performance of the simulation on the days with observations, for example with the Nash-Sutcliffe and Kling-Gupta efficiencies:

ok <- !is.na(ts$flow_obs) & !is.na(ts$flow_sim)
obs <- ts$flow_obs[ok]
sim <- ts$flow_sim[ok]

nse <- 1 - sum((sim - obs)^2) / sum((obs - mean(obs))^2)
kge <- 1 - sqrt((cor(sim, obs) - 1)^2 +
                  (sd(sim) / sd(obs) - 1)^2 +
                  (mean(sim) / mean(obs) - 1)^2)

round(c(NSE = nse, KGE = kge), 3)
#>   NSE   KGE 
#> 0.533 0.585

11. A simple water balance

Because precipitation, PET and streamflow are all in mm/day, a water balance can be computed directly. Using only the days with observed streamflow:

ok <- !is.na(ts$flow_obs)

balance <- data.frame(
  product = prec_cols,
  P = colMeans(ts[ok, prec_cols]),
  Q = mean(ts$flow_obs[ok]),
  row.names = NULL
)
balance$runoff_ratio <- balance$Q / balance$P
balance$aridity <- mean(ts$pet_hs[ok]) / balance$P
balance
#>         product        P         Q runoff_ratio   aridity
#> 1    prec_pisco 1.375481 0.5634122    0.4096111 2.4793629
#> 2   prec_chirps 1.238451 0.5634122    0.4549332 2.7536957
#> 3 prec_era5land 3.667580 0.5634122    0.1536196 0.9298546

A runoff ratio close to or above 1 points to an underestimation of precipitation by the product, a common issue in high mountain catchments.

12. Typical workflow with the full dataset 

library(RCamelsPE)

# Download once, or set the path of a local copy
# download_camels_pe(path = "path/to/folder")
set_camels_path("path/to/CAMELS-PE")

# Select near-natural catchments in the Pacific region
stations <- read_metadata()
attrs <- read_attributes("all")
sel <- attrs$gauge_id[attrs$near_natural == 1]
sel <- intersect(sel, stations$gauge_id[stations$gauge_region == "Pacific"])

# Read their forcing and streamflow
ts <- read_timeseries(
  gauge_id = sel,
  vars = c("date", "gauge_id", "prec_pisco", "prec_chirps",
           "prec_era5land", "pet_hs", "flow_obs", "flow_obs_flag")
)

# Annual land-cover change in the selected catchments
lc <- read_land_cover("class", gauge_id = sel, format = "long")
plot_land_cover(lc)

Summary

Function Purpose
download_camels_pe() Download the dataset from Zenodo
set_camels_path() Define the location of the dataset
read_dictionary() Variable descriptions, units and sources
read_metadata() Station metadata and quality-control summary
read_geospatial() Catchment boundaries and gauge locations
read_attributes() Static catchment attributes
read_land_cover() Annual land-cover series (class or subclass)
read_land_cover_legend() Land-cover legend
read_soil_classes() Soil suborders, great groups, horizon textures
read_soil_legend() Soil legend
read_timeseries() Daily time series
plot_timeseries() Time series plot
plot_catchments() Map of catchments and gauges
plot_attribute_map() Map of an attribute
plot_land_cover() Annual land-cover plot

To run this tutorial with the full dataset, download CAMELS-PE with download_camels_pe() or from Zenodo, and define its location with set_camels_path().
